title: 23.0 Basics
text:
Throughout this chapter:

Let \(k\) be a fixed base field.
A \(k\)-variety is defined as a geometrically reduced, separated scheme of finite type over \(k\).
We denote by \(\mathrm{Sch}/k\) the category of schemes of finite type over \(k\), and by \(\mathrm{Var}/k\) the full subcategory of \(k\)-varieties.
For an affine scheme \(X = \operatorname{Spec} A\), \(A\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-algebra.



Definition 1 (Algebraic Group and Abelian Variety)  

An algebraic group over \(k\) is a group object in the category \(\mathrm{Sch}/k\). That is, it is a scheme \(G\) of finite type over \(k\) equipped with \(k\)-morphisms:

Multiplication: \(m: G \times_k G \to G\),
Inverse: \(i: G \to G\),
Identity section: \(e: \operatorname{Spec} k \to G\),

satisfying the usual group axioms.
An abelian variety is an algebraic variety \(A \in \mathrm{Var}/k\) which is a proper, geometrically connected group object in \(\mathrm{Sch}/k\).



Lemma 1 (Smoothness of Geometrically Reduced Groups) Any geometrically reduced algebraic group \(G\) over \(k\) is smooth. Consequently, its connected components coincide with its irreducible components.


Proof. Proof sketch. Since \(G_{\bar{k}}\) is reduced and of finite type over an algebraically closed field, its smooth locus \(\operatorname{Sm}(G_{\bar{k}})\) is open and non-empty. For any closed point \(g \in G(\bar{k})\), the group translation \(L_g: G_{\bar{k}} \to G_{\bar{k}}\) is an automorphism mapping smooth points to smooth points. Transitivity of translations implies that every point of \(G_{\bar{k}}\) is smooth. Thus \(G\) is smooth over \(k\). Because smooth schemes are locally irreducible, the connected components must coincide with the irreducible components.


Lemma 2 (Rigidity Lemma) Let \(X, Y, Z\) be varieties over \(k\) with \(X\) proper and geometrically irreducible, and \(Y\) geometrically irreducible. Let \[
f: X \times_k Y \to Z
\] be a \(k\)-morphism. Suppose there exists a \(k\)-rational point \(y_0 \in Y(k)\) such that \(f(X \times \{y_0\}) = \{z_0\}\) for some \(z_0 \in Z(k)\).
Then \(f\) factors through the canonical projection \(p_2: X \times_k Y \to Y\). That is, there exists a morphism \(g: Y \to Z\) such that \(f = g \circ p_2\).


Proof. Fix a rational point \(x_0 \in X(k)\) (extending scalars to \(\bar{k}\) if necessary). Define \(g: Y \to Z\) by the composition: \[
Y \xrightarrow{x_0 \times \mathrm{id}_Y} X \times_k Y \xrightarrow{f} Z.
\] We show that \(f(x, y) = g(y)\) for all \(x \in X, y \in Y\).

Choose an affine open neighborhood \(U \subseteq Z\) containing \(z_0\). The complement \(Z \setminus U\) is closed in \(Z\), so \(f^{-1}(Z \setminus U)\) is closed in \(X \times_k Y\).
Since \(X\) is proper over \(k\), the projection \(p_2: X \times_k Y \to Y\) is universally closed. Thus: \[
W := p_2\big(f^{-1}(Z \setminus U)\big) = \{ y \in Y \mid \exists x \in X \text{ with } f(x, y) \notin U \}
\] is a closed subset of \(Y\).
By hypothesis, \(f(X \times \{y_0\}) = \{z_0\} \subseteq U\), so \(y_0 \notin W\). Hence \(Y \setminus W\) is an open neighborhood of \(y_0\). Pick an affine open neighborhood \(V \subseteq Y \setminus W\) containing \(y_0\).
By construction, \(f(X \times V) \subseteq U\). Since \(U\) is affine, we may choose a closed embedding \(U \hookrightarrow \mathbb{A}^n\). For every closed point \(y \in V\), the fiber \(X \times \{y\} \cong X\) is proper and connected. Its image in the affine space \(\mathbb{A}^n\) under \(f\) must be both proper and affine, hence it must be a single point: \[
f(X \times \{y\}) = \{f(x_0, y)\} = \{g(y)\}.
\]
Therefore, \(f|_{X \times V} = (g \circ p_2)|_{X \times V}\). Because \(X \times_k Y\) is reduced and \(Z\) is separated, two morphisms agreeing on a non-empty open subscheme are identical everywhere (Reduced-to-Separated Theorem). Thus \(f = g \circ p_2\).



Proposition 1 (Proper Connected Groups are Abelian) Any proper connected smooth algebraic group \(G\) over \(k\) is abelian. In particular, abelian varieties are commutative.


Proof. Consider the commutator morphism: \[
f: G \times_k G \to G, \quad (x, y) \mapsto x y x^{-1} y^{-1}.
\] Observe that \(f(G \times \{e\}) = \{e\}\). Since \(G\) is proper and connected, Lemma 2 implies that \(f\) factors through the projection to the second factor: \[
f(x, y) = f(e, y) = e y e^{-1} y^{-1} = e.
\] Hence \(xyx^{-1}y^{-1} = e\) for all \(x, y \in G\), meaning \(xy = yx\). Thus \(G\) is abelian.



Proposition 2 (Separatedness of Group Schemes) Every group scheme \(G\) of finite type over a field \(k\) is separated.


Proof. A morphism \(G \to \operatorname{Spec} k\) is separated if and only if the diagonal \(\Delta: G \to G \times_k G\) is a closed immersion.
Consider the difference morphism \(\mu: G \times_k G \to G\) defined by \((g_1, g_2) \mapsto g_1 g_2^{-1}\). The diagonal \(\Delta(G)\) is the scheme-theoretic pullback of the identity section \(e: \operatorname{Spec} k \to G\) along \(\mu\): \[
\begin{CD}
G @>{\Delta}>> G \times_k G \\
@VVV @VV{\mu}V \\
\operatorname{Spec} k @>{e}>> G
\end{CD}
\] Because base change preserves closed immersions, it suffices to prove that \(e: \operatorname{Spec} k \to G\) is a closed immersion. The image of \(e\) is a single point \(e \in G\). Since \(G\) is of finite type over \(k\), the point \(e\) has residue field \(k(e) \cong k\) and is closed. Thus \(e\) is a closed immersion, which implies \(\Delta\) is a closed immersion. Therefore, \(G\) is separated over \(k\).


Lemma 3 (Open Subgroups are Closed)  

If \(G\) is a group scheme over \(k\) such that \(G_{\mathrm{red}} \times_k G_{\mathrm{red}}\) is reduced, then \(G_{\mathrm{red}} \hookrightarrow G\) is a closed subgroup scheme. In particular, if \(G_{\mathrm{red}}\) is geometrically reduced (e.g., if \(k\) is perfect), then \(G_{\mathrm{red}} \hookrightarrow G\) is a smooth closed subgroup scheme of \(G\).
Let \(\varphi: G' \to G\) be a homomorphism of group schemes over \(k\). If the image \(\varphi(G')\) is open in \(G\), then \(\varphi(G')\) is also closed in \(G\).



Proof. Proof of (2). Let \(U = \varphi(G') \subseteq G\) be open. Endow the complement \(Z := G \setminus U\) with the reduced subscheme structure. It suffices to show that \(Z\) is open.
Consider the action map \(Z \times_k G' \to G\) given by \((z, g') \mapsto z \cdot \varphi(g')\). For any \(g' \in G'\), the translation \(x \mapsto x \cdot \varphi(g')\) is an automorphism of \(G\). Since \(U = \varphi(G')\) is stable under right multiplication by \(\varphi(G')\), its complement \(Z\) is also stable under multiplication by \(\varphi(G')\).
Because translations are open morphisms, the image of \(Z \times_k G' \to G\) is a union of translates of \(Z\), which is open. But this image is precisely \(Z\) itself. Hence \(Z\) is open, which proves \(U = G \setminus Z\) is closed.


Lemma 4 (Immersions of Group Schemes are Closed) Let \(i: G' \hookrightarrow G\) be an immersion of group schemes over \(k\). Then \(i\) is a closed immersion.


Proof. Without loss of generality, assume \(G\) and \(G'\) are reduced. Let \(\overline{G'}\) denote the scheme-theoretic closure of \(i(G')\) in \(G\) equipped with the reduced structure. Since multiplication \(m: G \times_k G \to G\) is continuous and maps \(G' \times_k G'\) into \(G'\), it maps the closure \(\overline{G'} \times_k \overline{G'}\) into \(\overline{G'}\). Thus \(\overline{G'}\) is a closed subgroup scheme of \(G\).
Since \(i\) is an immersion, \(i(G')\) is an open subscheme of \(\overline{G'}\). By Lemma 3, an open subgroup scheme of \(\overline{G'}\) is closed in \(\overline{G'}\). Hence \(i(G') = \overline{G'}\), so \(i(G')\) is closed in \(G\).


Lemma 5 (Connected Implies Irreducible) Let \(G\) be a group scheme of finite type over \(k\).

If \(G\) is irreducible, then \(G\) is quasi-compact.
If \(G\) is connected, then \(G\) is irreducible.


(Reference: The Stacks Project, Tag 047R, Tag 047S).


Proposition 3 (Subgroup Schemes and Kernels)  

A closed subscheme \(H \subseteq G\) is a normal subgroup scheme (denoted \(H \trianglelefteq G\)) if for all \(T \in \mathrm{Sch}/k\), \(H(T)\) is a normal subgroup of \(G(T)\) (equivalently, \(H(R) \trianglelefteq G(R)\) for all \(R \in \mathrm{Alg}_k\)).
Let \(\varphi: G \to G'\) be a homomorphism of group schemes. The scheme-theoretic kernel is defined as the fiber product: \[
\ker \varphi := \operatorname{Spec} k \times_{e, G', \varphi} G = \varphi^{-1}(e).
\] Then \(\ker \varphi\) is a closed normal subgroup scheme of \(G\).
On functor of points, \(\ker(\varphi)(R) = \ker(G(R) \to G'(R))\) for all \(R \in \mathrm{Alg}_k\).



Proposition 4 (Homomorphisms and Dimensions) Let \(\varphi: G \to G'\) be a homomorphism of algebraic groups over \(k\).

The scheme-theoretic image \(\varphi(G)\) is closed in \(G'\). We denote \(\operatorname{Im} \varphi := \varphi(G)_{\mathrm{red}}\).
Dimension Formula: \[
\dim G = \dim \ker \varphi + \dim \operatorname{Im} \varphi.
\]



Proof. Idea of Proof. By Chevalley’s Theorem on constructible sets, \(\varphi(G)\) contains a dense open subset of its closure. Group translations then show that \(\varphi(G)\) is open in its closure \(\overline{\varphi(G)}\). By Lemma 3, an open subgroup of \(\overline{\varphi(G)}\) is closed, whence \(\varphi(G) = \overline{\varphi(G)}\).


Proposition 5 (Image Factorization and Flatness)  

If \(G'\) is reduced and \(\varphi: G \to G'\) is dominant, then \(\varphi\) is an fppf morphism (faithfully flat locally of finite presentation).
If \(G\) is smooth, any homomorphism \(\varphi: G \to H\) factors canonically as: \[
G \xrightarrow{p} I \xrightarrow{i} H
\] where \(p\) is fppf and \(i\) is a closed immersion into \(H\).



Proof. Set \(I := \varphi(G)\) with reduced subscheme structure. By generic flatness, there exists a dense open subscheme \(U \subseteq I\) over which \(\varphi^{-1}(U) \to U\) is flat. Since translations by rational points (over \(\bar{k}\)) act transitively on \(I\), translates of \(U\) cover \(I\). Therefore, \(\varphi_{\bar{k}}\) is flat everywhere. Being surjective (image is closed) between noetherian schemes, it is fppf.



Remark 1 (Hopf Algebras and Functor of Points). An affine scheme \(G = \operatorname{Spec} A\) is a group scheme if and only if its coordinate ring \(A = \mathcal{O}(G)\) is a commutative Hopf algebra over \(k\), equipped with:

Comultiplication \(\Delta: A \to A \otimes_k A\),
Counit \(\varepsilon: A \to k\),
Antipode \(S: A \to A\).

We have an anti-equivalence of categories: \[
\{\text{Commutative f.g. Hopf } k\text{-algebras}\}^{\mathrm{op}} \xrightarrow{\sim} \{\text{Affine / Linear } k\text{-algebraic groups}\}.
\]
Via the functor of points, the Yoneda embedding yields a fully faithful functor: \[
\mathbf{GrpSch}/k \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Fun}(\mathrm{Alg}_k, \mathbf{Grp}), \quad G \mapsto (R \mapsto G(R) = \operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(A, R)).
\]


Example 1 (Basic Examples)  

Finite Constant Group: Let \(\Gamma\) be a finite abstract group. The coordinate algebra is \(A = \prod_{g \in \Gamma} k \cdot e_g\) with orthogonal idempotents \(e_g\).

Comultiplication: \(\Delta(e_x) = \sum_{yz = x} e_y \otimes e_z\),
Antipode: \(S(e_x) = e_{x^{-1}}\),
Counit: \(\varepsilon(e_x) = \delta_{x, e}\).

On \(R\)-points: \[
G(R) = \left\{ (r_g)_{g \in \Gamma} \in R^\Gamma \;\middle|\; \sum_{g \in \Gamma} r_g = 1, \, r_g r_h = 0 \text{ for } g \neq h \right\}.
\]
Standard Matrix Groups (for \(n \in \mathbb{N}\)):

General Linear Group \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) (Reductive): \[
\mathrm{GL}_n(R) = \{ M \in \mathrm{Mat}_{n \times n}(R) \mid \det(M) \in R^\times \}.
\]
Standard Borel Subgroup \(B_n\) (Solvable): \[
B_n(R) = \{ (x_{ij}) \in \mathrm{GL}_n(R) \mid x_{ij} = 0 \text{ for all } i > j \}.
\]
Standard Unipotent Subgroup \(U_n\) (Unipotent): \[
U_n(R) = \{ (x_{ij}) \in B_n(R) \mid x_{ii} = 1 \text{ for all } 1 \le i \le n \}.
\]
Standard Maximal Torus \(T_n\) (Split Torus): \[
T_n(R) = \{ (x_{ij}) \in B_n(R) \mid x_{ij} = 0 \text{ for all } i \neq j \} \cong (\mathbb{G}_{m, R})^n.
\]

These satisfy the inclusion hierarchy: \[
U_n \trianglelefteq B_n \subseteq \mathrm{GL}_n, \quad T_n \subseteq B_n, \quad B_n = T_n \ltimes U_n.
\]




Proposition 6 (Existence of the Largest Étale Subalgebra) Let \(X\) be a scheme of finite type over \(k\). Then there exists a unique largest étale \(k\)-subalgebra \(\pi_0(X) \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\).


Proof. 

If \(A_1, A_2 \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\) are étale \(k\)-subalgebras, the subring generated by them is the image of the canonical map \(A_1 \otimes_k A_2 \to \mathcal{O}(X)\). Since the tensor product of étale algebras is étale and any quotient of an étale algebra over a field is étale, the composite is étale.
For any étale subalgebra \(A \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\), base change to the separable closure satisfies: \[
A \otimes_k k^{\mathrm{sep}} \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X) \otimes_k k^{\mathrm{sep}} = \mathcal{O}(X_{k^{\mathrm{sep}}}).
\] Since \(A \otimes_k k^{\mathrm{sep}} \cong \prod_{i=1}^m k^{\mathrm{sep}}\), it admits a complete system of orthogonal idempotents \(e_1, \dots, e_m\). Each \(e_i\) defines a non-empty open and closed subscheme \(V(1 - e_i)\) of \(X_{k^{\mathrm{sep}}}\). Thus \(m \le \#\{\text{connected components of } X_{k^{\mathrm{sep}}}\}\).
Because \(X\) is of finite type, it has finitely many connected components. The dimension \(\dim_k A\) is uniformly bounded, guaranteeing the existence of a unique maximal étale subalgebra.



Definition 2 (The Scheme \(\pi_0(X)\))  

Let \(A \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\) be the largest étale \(k\)-subalgebra. We define: \[
\pi_0(X) := \operatorname{Spec} A.
\] The inclusion \(A \hookrightarrow \mathcal{O}(X)\) induces a canonical morphism \(X \to \pi_0(X)\).
Universal Property: For any étale \(k\)-scheme \(Y\) and any \(k\)-morphism \(f: X \to Y\), there exists a unique morphism \(\bar{f}: \pi_0(X) \to Y\) such that the following diagram commutes: \[
\begin{CD}
X @>{f}>> Y \\
@VVV @| \\
\pi_0(X) @>{\exists! \bar{f}}>> Y
\end{CD}
\]
Properties:

The fibers of \(X \to \pi_0(X)\) are the connected components of \(X\).
For every \(y \in \pi_0(X)\), the fiber \(X_y\) is geometrically connected over the residue field \(k(y)\).
\(\pi_0\) preserves finite products: \(\pi_0(X \times_k Y) \cong \pi_0(X) \times_k \pi_0(Y)\).
The canonical morphism \(X \to \pi_0(X)\) is fppf.




Proposition 7 (Geometric Connectedness Criteria)  

If \(X\) is connected and \(X(k) \neq \emptyset\), then \(X\) is geometrically connected.
If \(X\) is geometrically connected and \(Y\) is connected, then \(X \times_k Y\) is connected.



Proof. 

If \(X\) is connected, \(\pi_0(X) = \operatorname{Spec} L\), where \(L/k\) is a finite separable field extension. A rational point \(x \in X(k)\) provides a section \(\operatorname{Spec} k \to X \to \operatorname{Spec} L\), forcing \(L \cong k\). Thus \(\pi_0(X) = \operatorname{Spec} k\), so \(X\) is geometrically connected.
We have \(\pi_0(X) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k\). By product preservation, \[
\pi_0(X \times_k Y) \cong \pi_0(X) \times_k \pi_0(Y) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k \times_k \pi_0(Y) \cong \pi_0(Y).
\] Since \(Y\) is connected, \(\pi_0(Y) = \operatorname{Spec} L\) for a field \(L\). Thus \(\pi_0(X \times_k Y) \cong \operatorname{Spec} L\), which shows \(X \times_k Y\) is connected.



Definition 3 (The Identity Component \(G^\circ\))  

The identity component \(G^\circ\) of an algebraic group \(G\) is the connected component containing the identity section \(e\). Endowed with its open subscheme structure, \(G^\circ\) is a smooth, geometrically connected, open and closed normal subgroup scheme of \(G\).
For any open subgroup \(G' \subseteq G\) of finite index, \(G^\circ \subseteq G' \subseteq G\), and \((G^\circ)^\circ = G^\circ\).



Proposition 8 (\(\pi_0(G)\) and the Connected Component) Let \(G\) be an algebraic group over \(k\).

\(\pi_0(G)\) is a finite étale group scheme over \(k\), and the canonical morphism \(G \to \pi_0(G)\) is a homomorphism of algebraic groups.
The identity component \(G^\circ := \ker(G \to \pi_0(G))\) is a geometrically connected, normal closed and open subgroup scheme of \(G\). For any field extension \(L/k\), we have \((G_L)^\circ = (G^\circ)_L\).
\(G\) is connected \(\iff \pi_0(G) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k \iff G\) is geometrically connected.
Formation of the identity component commutes with products: \((G \times_k H)^\circ \cong G^\circ \times_k H^\circ\).
If \(H\) is a connected group scheme over \(k\), any homomorphism \(\psi: H \to G\) factors uniquely through \(G^\circ \hookrightarrow G\).



Proof. 

Since \(\pi_0\) commutes with finite products, the group morphisms \(m, i, e\) on \(G\) induce group structure morphisms on \(\pi_0(G)\) by functoriality.
For (3), since \(e \in G^\circ(k)\), \(G^\circ\) has a \(k\)-rational point. Proposition 7(1) implies that \(G^\circ\) is geometrically connected.
For (5), since \(H\) is connected, \(\pi_0(H) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k\). Functoriality yields a commutative diagram: \[
\begin{CD}
H @>{\psi}>> G \\
@VVV @VVV \\
\pi_0(H) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k @>{e}>> \pi_0(G)
\end{CD}
\] Thus the composition \(H \to G \to \pi_0(G)\) is the trivial map, which implies that \(\psi\) factors uniquely through \(G^\circ = \ker(G \to \pi_0(G))\).



Definition 4 (Exact Sequences of Group Schemes) A sequence of homomorphisms of group schemes over \(k\): \[
1 \longrightarrow N \xrightarrow{\quad i \quad} G \xrightarrow{\quad p \quad} Q \longrightarrow 1
\] is said to be exact if:

\(i: N \hookrightarrow G\) is a closed immersion identifying \(N\) with a normal subgroup scheme of \(G\);
\(p: G \to Q\) is an fppf morphism;
\(i(N) = \ker(p)\).

title: 22.2 Cones
text:
Definition 1 (Ample and Nef Cones) Let \(X\) be a complete variety over \(k\).

The ample cone of \(X\), denoted by \(\operatorname{Amp}(X) \subseteq N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\), is the open convex cone generated by all ample \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor classes on \(X\).
The nef cone of \(X\), denoted by \(\operatorname{Nef}(X) \subseteq N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\), is the closed convex cone consisting of all nef \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor classes on \(X\).
By Kleiman’s criterion and openness of amplitude, the nef cone is the closure of the ample cone, and the ample cone is the interior of the nef cone: \[
\operatorname{Nef}(X) = \overline{\operatorname{Amp}(X)}, \qquad \operatorname{Amp}(X) = \operatorname{Nef}(X)^\circ.
\]



Definition 2 (The Cone of Effective Curves \(\operatorname{NE}(X)\)) Let \(X\) be a complete variety.

The cone of effective curves is the convex cone: \[
\operatorname{NE}(X) := \sum_{C \subseteq X} \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} [C] \subseteq N_1(X)_{\mathbb{R}},
\] where \(C\) runs over all irreducible curves on \(X\).
The closed cone of curves is denoted by \(\overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)\). Under the perfect pairing \(N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} \times N_1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} \to \mathbb{R}\), it is dual to the nef cone: \[
\overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X) = \big\{ \gamma \in N_1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} \;\big|\; (\delta \cdot \gamma) \ge 0, \; \forall \delta \in \operatorname{Nef}(X) \big\}.
\]
For an \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor \(D \in \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{R}}(X)\), let \(\phi_D: N_1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} \to \mathbb{R}\) be the linear functional \(\gamma \mapsto (\gamma \cdot D)\). We write: \[
D^\perp := \ker(\phi_D), \qquad D_{\ge 0} := \phi_D^{-1}(\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}), \qquad D_{> 0} := \phi_D^{-1}(\mathbb{R}_{> 0}).
\]



Lemma 1 (Slicing Criterion for Amplitude) Let \(X\) be a projective variety (or scheme) and \(H\) an ample \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor on \(X\). An \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor \(D\) on \(X\) is ample if and only if there exists \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that: \[
\frac{(D \cdot C)}{(H \cdot C)} \ge \varepsilon \quad \text{for all irreducible curves } C \subseteq X.
\]


Proof. \((\impliedby)\): We write \(D = (D - \varepsilon H) + \varepsilon H\). By assumption, for every irreducible curve \(C \subseteq X\), \[
((D - \varepsilon H) \cdot C) = (D \cdot C) - \varepsilon (H \cdot C) \ge 0,
\] which means \(D - \varepsilon H\) is nef. Since \(\varepsilon H\) is ample, Kleiman’s perturbation theorem implies that \(D = (D - \varepsilon H) + \varepsilon H\) is ample.
\((\implies)\): If \(D\) is ample, by the openness of the ample cone, \(D - \varepsilon H\) remains ample for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon > 0\). In particular, for any curve \(C \subseteq X\), \[
((D - \varepsilon H) \cdot C) > 0 \implies (D \cdot C) > \varepsilon (H \cdot C),
\] whence \(\frac{(D \cdot C)}{(H \cdot C)} \ge \varepsilon\).


Theorem 1 (Amplitude via Cones (Kleiman’s Criterion)) Let \(X\) be a projective variety, and let \(D \in \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{R}}(X)\). Then \(D\) is ample if and only if: \[
\overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X) \setminus \{0\} \subseteq D_{> 0},
\] that is, \((\gamma \cdot D) > 0\) for every non-zero class \(\gamma \in \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X) \setminus \{0\}\).


Proof. \((\impliedby)\): Consider the linear functional \(\phi_D: N_1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} \to \mathbb{R}\), \(\gamma \mapsto (\gamma \cdot D)\). By hypothesis, \(\phi_D(\gamma) > 0\) for all \(\gamma \in \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X) \setminus \{0\}\).
Choose ample divisors \(H_1, \dots, H_r\) on \(X\) whose classes form a basis of \(N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\). Since the intersection pairing is non-degenerate, \[
\|\gamma\| := \sum_{i=1}^r |(H_i \cdot \gamma)|
\] defines a norm on \(N_1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\). Consider the compact unit sphere \(S := \{ \gamma \in N_1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} \mid \|\gamma\| = 1 \}\). The intersection \(\overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X) \cap S\) is compact and does not contain \(0\). Therefore, \(\phi_D\) attains a strictly positive minimum on this set: \[
\phi_D(\gamma) \ge \varepsilon > 0 \quad \text{for all } \gamma \in \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X) \cap S.
\] By linearity, \((D \cdot \gamma) \ge \varepsilon \|\gamma\|\) for all \(\gamma \in \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)\). For any curve \(C \subseteq X\), since each \(H_i\) is ample, \((H_i \cdot C) > 0\), so \(\|[C]\| = \sum_{i=1}^r (H_i \cdot C) = (H \cdot C)\), where \(H = \sum_{i=1}^r H_i\) is ample. Thus: \[
(D \cdot C) \ge \varepsilon (H \cdot C) \implies \frac{(D \cdot C)}{(H \cdot C)} \ge \varepsilon.
\] By Lemma 1, \(D\) is ample.
\((\implies)\): Suppose \(D\) is ample. Fix \(H = \sum_{i=1}^r H_i\) as above. By openness of amplitude, \(D - \varepsilon H\) is ample for some \(\varepsilon > 0\). Hence \(D - \varepsilon H\) is nef, which implies: \[
(\gamma \cdot (D - \varepsilon H)) \ge 0 \quad \text{for all } \gamma \in \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X).
\] For every \(\gamma \in \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X) \cap S\), we have \((\gamma \cdot H) = \|\gamma\| = 1\), hence: \[
(\gamma \cdot D) \ge \varepsilon (\gamma \cdot H) = \varepsilon > 0.
\] Thus \(\overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X) \setminus \{0\} \subseteq D_{> 0}\).


Remark 1 (Effective Curves are Not Enough). The condition \((D \cdot C) > 0\) for every irreducible effective curve \(C \subseteq X\) is not sufficient to guarantee that \(D\) is ample: \[
D \text{ ample} \centernot\iff \forall \text{ curve } C \subseteq X, \; (D \cdot C) > 0.
\] One must test all classes in the closure \(\overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)\) (e.g., Mumford’s famous construction of a non-ample divisor positive on all curves).


Theorem 2 (Openness of Amplitude in Families) Let \(f: X \to T\) be a proper morphism of schemes, and let \(L\) be a line bundle on \(X\). Then the locus: \[
V := \big\{ t \in T \;\big|\; L_t \text{ is ample on } X_t \big\}
\] is an open subset of \(T\).


Proof. Being an open property is local on \(T\), so we may assume \(T = \operatorname{Spec} A\) is affine. It suffices to show that if \(0 \in T\) is a point such that \(L_0\) is ample on \(X_0 = f^{-1}(0)\), then there exists an open neighborhood \(U \subseteq T\) of \(0\) such that \(L_t\) is ample on \(X_t\) for all \(t \in U\).
Step 1: Vanishing of higher pushforwards. We claim that for any \(\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Coh}(X)\), there exists an integer \(m(\mathcal{F}, L) > 0\) such that for all \(i \ge 1\) and all \(m \ge m(\mathcal{F}, L)\), \[
R^i f_*(\mathcal{F} \otimes L^{\otimes m}) = 0 \quad \text{in an open neighborhood of } 0.
\] For \(i > \dim X_0\), upper semicontinuity of fiber dimensions implies \(\dim X_t \le \dim X_0 < i\) for \(t\) near \(0\), so \(H^i(X_t, \mathcal{F}_t \otimes L_t^{\otimes m}) = 0\). By the Theorem on Formal Functions, \((R^i f_*(\mathcal{F} \otimes L^{\otimes m}))_0^\wedge = 0\), hence \(R^i f_*(\mathcal{F} \otimes L^{\otimes m}) = 0\) in an open neighborhood of \(0\).
We proceed by decreasing induction on \(i\). Assume the claim holds for index \(i\); we establish it for \(i - 1\). First, assume \(0\) is a closed point with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}_0 \subseteq A\). Choose generators \(u_1, \dots, u_p \in \mathfrak{m}_0\). This gives an exact sequence: \[
A^{\oplus p} \xrightarrow{\quad (u_j) \quad} A \longrightarrow A/\mathfrak{m}_0 \longrightarrow 0.
\] Pulling back and tensoring with \(\mathcal{F}\), we obtain: \[
0 \longrightarrow \mathcal{K} \longrightarrow \mathcal{F}^{\oplus p} \xrightarrow{\quad (f^* u_j) \quad} \mathcal{F} \longrightarrow \mathcal{F} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{O}_{X_0} \longrightarrow 0.
\] Let \(\mathcal{I} = \operatorname{Im}(f^* u_j)\). By the induction hypothesis, \(R^i f_*(\mathcal{K} \otimes L^{\otimes m}) = 0\) near \(0\) for \(m \gg 0\). Furthermore, because \(L_0\) is ample on \(X_0\), Serre vanishing gives \(H^{i-1}(X_0, \mathcal{F}_0 \otimes L_0^{\otimes m}) = 0\) for \(m \gg 0\), hence \(R^{i-1} f_*(\mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{O}_{X_0} \otimes L^{\otimes m}) = 0\).
From the exact sequence \(0 \to \mathcal{I} \to \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{O}_{X_0} \to 0\), the map \(R^{i-1} f_*(\mathcal{I} \otimes L^{\otimes m}) \to R^{i-1} f_*(\mathcal{F} \otimes L^{\otimes m})\) is surjective at \(0\). Combining with the surjection \(\mathcal{F}^{\oplus p} \twoheadrightarrow \mathcal{I}\), the map: \[
\big(R^{i-1} f_*(\mathcal{F} \otimes L^{\otimes m})\big)^{\oplus p} \xrightarrow{\quad (u_j) \quad} R^{i-1} f_*(\mathcal{F} \otimes L^{\otimes m})
\] has image equal to \(\mathfrak{m}_0 \cdot R^{i-1} f_*(\mathcal{F} \otimes L^{\otimes m})\). At the stalk at \(0\): \[
\mathfrak{m}_0 \big(R^{i-1} f_*(\mathcal{F} \otimes L^{\otimes m})\big)_0 = \big(R^{i-1} f_*(\mathcal{F} \otimes L^{\otimes m})\big)_0.
\] By Nakayama’s Lemma, \((R^{i-1} f_*(\mathcal{F} \otimes L^{\otimes m}))_0 = 0\). Since this sheaf is coherent, it vanishes on an open neighborhood of \(0\).
Step 2: Relative global generation and finiteness. Consider the ideal sheaf \(\mathcal{I}_{X_0/X}\) of \(X_0\) in \(X\). For \(m \gg 0\), Step 1 gives \(R^1 f_*(\mathcal{I}_{X_0/X} \otimes L^{\otimes m}) = 0\) near \(0\). Hence: \[
f_* L^{\otimes m} \longrightarrow f_*(L^{\otimes m} \otimes \mathcal{O}_{X_0}) = H^0(X_0, L_0^{\otimes m})
\] is surjective near \(0\). Since \(L_0\) is ample, \(L_0^{\otimes m}\) is globally generated on \(X_0\) for \(m \gg 0\). Thus the canonical evaluation: \[
\rho_m: f^* f_* L^{\otimes m} \longrightarrow L^{\otimes m}
\] is surjective when restricted to \(X_0\). By Nakayama’s Lemma, \(\operatorname{coker}(\rho_m)\) vanishes on an open neighborhood of \(X_0\). Because \(f\) is proper, \(U_m := T \setminus f(\operatorname{Supp} \operatorname{coker} \rho_m)\) is an open neighborhood of \(0\). Shrinking \(T\), we may assume \(\rho_m\) is surjective everywhere on \(X\).
Thus \(L^{\otimes m}\) is relatively generated by global sections over \(T\), inducing a \(T\)-morphism: \[
\phi: X \longrightarrow \mathbb{P}_T^N.
\] On the fiber \(X_0\), \(\phi|_{X_0}: X_0 \to \mathbb{P}_{k(0)}^N\) is an immersion, hence finite. The locus of points where the fibers of \(\phi\) have dimension 0: \[
F := \big\{ x \in X \;\big|\; \dim_x \phi^{-1}(\phi(x)) = 0 \big\}
\] is open in \(X\) by upper semicontinuity of fiber dimensions, and contains \(X_0\). Since \(f\) is proper, \(U := T \setminus f(X \setminus F)\) is an open neighborhood of \(0\). The restricted morphism \(\phi|_{f^{-1}(U)}: f^{-1}(U) \to \mathbb{P}_U^N\) is proper and quasi-finite. By Zariski’s Main Theorem, it is finite. Consequently, \(L_t\) is ample on \(X_t\) for all \(t \in U\).
Non-closed points: If \(0\) is not closed, consider the local ring \(\mathcal{O}_{T, 0}\). By flat base change, the cohomology stalks match. Applying the above argument to the closed point of \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{T, 0}\) produces the desired vanishing and openness, concluding the proof.


Corollary 1 (Fiber-Wise Amplitude)  

Let \(f: X \to T\) be a proper morphism and \(L\) a line bundle on \(X\). If \(L_t\) is ample on \(X_t\) for all \(t\) in a dense subset \(S \subseteq T\), then the ample locus contains an open dense subset. If \(L_t\) is ample for all \(t \in T\), then \(L\) is \(f\)-relatively ample.
If \(\psi: X \to \mathbb{P}_T(\mathcal{E})\) is a finite morphism over \(T\), then \(\psi^* \mathcal{O}(1)\) is \(f\)-ample.



Corollary 2 (Relative Nakai-Moishezon Criterion) Let \(f: X \to T\) be a proper morphism and \(D\) a \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisor on \(X\). Then \(D\) is \(f\)-ample if and only if for every closed point \(t \in T\) and every irreducible subvariety \(V \subseteq X_t\) with \(\dim V \ge 1\), \[
(D^{\dim V} \cdot V) > 0.
\]


Proposition 1 (Relative and Absolute Amplitude) Let \(f: X \to T\) be a morphism of proper schemes, \(L\) a line bundle on \(X\), and \(A\) an ample line bundle on \(T\). Then \(L\) is \(f\)-ample if and only if \(L \otimes f^* A^{\otimes m}\) is ample on \(X\) for all \(m \gg 0\).


Proof. \((\implies)\): If \(L\) is \(f\)-ample, then for \(k \gg 0\), \(f^* f_* L^{\otimes k} \twoheadrightarrow L^{\otimes k}\). Since \(A\) is ample on \(T\), \(f_* L^{\otimes k} \otimes A^{\otimes m}\) is globally generated for \(m \gg 0\). Choosing a surjection \(\mathcal{O}_T^{\oplus p} \twoheadrightarrow f_* L^{\otimes k} \otimes A^{\otimes m}\), we obtain a surjection \(\mathcal{O}_X^{\oplus p} \twoheadrightarrow L^{\otimes k} \otimes f^* A^{\otimes m}\), which defines a morphism: \[
X \longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{p-1} \times T.
\] Over each \(t \in T\), the restricted map \(X_t \to \mathbb{P}_{k(t)}^{p-1}\) is finite since \(L_t\) is ample. Hence \(X \to \mathbb{P}^{p-1} \times T\) is quasi-finite and proper, hence finite. Thus \(L^{\otimes k} \otimes f^* A^{\otimes m}\) is ample, which implies \(L \otimes f^* A^{\otimes m'}\) is ample for large \(m'\).
\((\impliedby)\): If \(L \otimes f^* A^{\otimes m}\) is ample on \(X\), its restriction to each fiber \(X_t\) is ample. But \((f^* A)|_{X_t} \cong \mathcal{O}_{X_t}\), so \((L \otimes f^* A^{\otimes m})|_{X_t} \cong L_t\). Hence \(L_t\) is ample for all \(t\), so \(L\) is \(f\)-ample by Corollary 1.


Definition 3 (Relative Nefness) Let \(f: X \to T\) be a proper morphism. A line bundle \(L\) on \(X\) is \(f\)-nef if \(L_t\) is nef on \(X_t\) for every \(t \in T\). Equivalently, \((L \cdot C) \ge 0\) for every irreducible curve \(C \subseteq X\) mapped to a point by \(f\).


Lemma 2 (Higher Cohomology of Nef Divisors) Let \(X\) be a projective scheme of dimension \(n\), and let \(D\) be a nef Cartier divisor on \(X\). Then for any coherent sheaf \(\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Coh}(X)\) and every \(i \ge 1\), \[
h^i(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = O(m^{n-i}) \quad \text{as } m \to \infty.
\]


Proof. By standard filtering techniques, we reduce immediately to the case where \(X\) is an integral variety. We proceed by induction on \(n = \dim X\):

If \(n = 1\), the only higher cohomology is \(i = 1\), and \(h^1(X, \mathcal{F}(mD)) = O(1) = O(m^0)\) by Serre duality and Riemann-Roch for curves.
Assume the statement holds in dimension \(\le n - 1\).

Let \(r = \operatorname{rank} \mathcal{F}\). For \(p \gg 0\), \(\mathcal{F}(p)\) is generically generated by \(r\) sections, yielding an exact sequence: \[
0 \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X(-p)^{\oplus r} \longrightarrow \mathcal{F} \longrightarrow \mathcal{C} \longrightarrow 0,
\] where \(\dim \operatorname{Supp}(\mathcal{C}) \le n - 1\). By the induction hypothesis, \(h^i(X, \mathcal{C} \otimes \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = O(m^{n-1-i}) = O(m^{n-i})\). Thus it suffices to prove the result for \(\mathcal{O}_X(-p)\), and slicing by a hyperplane reduces it to proving the theorem for \(\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{O}_X\).
Write \(D \sim A - B\) with \(A, B\) effective very ample divisors. Tensoring the defining sequences of \(A\) and \(B\): \[
0 \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X(mD - B) \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X((m+1)D) \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_A((m+1)D) \longrightarrow 0,
\] \[
0 \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X(mD - B) \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X(mD) \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_B(mD) \longrightarrow 0.
\] For \(i \ge 2\), applying the induction hypothesis to the \((n-1)\)-dimensional subvarieties \(A\) and \(B\) gives: \[
|h^i(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) - h^i(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD - B))| \le h^i(B, \mathcal{O}_B(mD)) = O(m^{n-1-i}) = O(m^{n-i}).
\] Similarly, \(|h^i(X, \mathcal{O}_X((m+1)D)) - h^i(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD - B))| = O(m^{n-i})\). Hence: \[
|h^i(X, \mathcal{O}_X((m+1)D)) - h^i(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD))| = O(m^{n-1-i}),
\] which integrates to \(h^i(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = O(m^{n-i})\) for all \(i \ge 2\).
For \(i = 1\): by Asymptotic Riemann-Roch I (?@thm-asymptotic-rr-1), \[
\chi(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) - h^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) + O(m^{n-2}) = \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}).
\] - If \(h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = 0\) for all \(m \gg 0\), then \(-h^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}) \le 0\). Since \(D\) is nef, Kleiman’s Theorem forces \((D^n) \ge 0\), whence \((D^n) = 0\), giving \(h^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = O(m^{n-1})\). - If \(h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(m_0 D)) > 0\) for some \(m_0 > 0\), choose an effective section \(E \in |m_0 D|\) and consider: \[
  0 \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X((m - m_0)D) \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X(mD) \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_E(mD) \longrightarrow 0.
  \] Applying the induction hypothesis to the subvariety \(E\) of dimension \(n - 1\): \[
  h^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) - h^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X((m - m_0)D)) \le h^1(E, \mathcal{O}_E(mD)) = O(m^{n-2}).
  \] Summing telescopically over \(m\) proves \(h^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = O(m^{n-1})\).


Proposition 2 (Asymptotic Riemann-Roch III (for Nef Divisors)) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety of dimension \(n\), and let \(D\) be a nef divisor on \(X\). For every coherent sheaf \(\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Coh}(X)\), \[
h^0(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = \operatorname{rank}(\mathcal{F}) \cdot \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}).
\]


Theorem 3 (Generalized Hodge Inequality) Let \(X\) be an irreducible complex projective variety of dimension \(n\). For any nef classes \(\delta_1, \dots, \delta_n \in \operatorname{Nef}(X) \subseteq N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\), \[
(\delta_1 \cdots \delta_n)^n \ge (\delta_1^n) \cdots (\delta_n^n).
\]


Corollary 3 (Khovanskii-Teissier and Brunn-Minkowski Inequalities) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety of dimension \(n\).

For nef classes \(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_p, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_{n-p} \in \operatorname{Nef}(X)\): \[
(\alpha_1 \cdots \alpha_p \cdot \beta_1 \cdots \beta_{n-p})^p \ge \prod_{i=1}^p (\alpha_i^p \cdot \beta_1 \cdots \beta_{n-p}).
\]
For any two nef classes \(\alpha, \beta \in \operatorname{Nef}(X)\) and any \(0 \le p \le n\): \[
(\alpha^p \cdot \beta^{n-p})^n \ge (\alpha^n)^p (\beta^n)^{n-p}.
\]
For any \(0 \le i \le n\): \[
(\alpha^i \cdot \beta^{n-i})^2 \ge (\alpha^{i+1} \cdot \beta^{n-i-1}) (\alpha^{i-1} \cdot \beta^{n-i+1}).
\]
Brunn-Minkowski Inequality: For any nef classes \(\alpha, \beta \in \operatorname{Nef}(X)\), \[
\big((\alpha + \beta)^n\big)^{1/n} \ge (\alpha^n)^{1/n} + (\beta^n)^{1/n}.
\]

title: 22.6 Graded Linear Series
text:
Definition 1 (Graded Linear Series) Let \(X\) be an irreducible variety over \(\mathbb{C}\).

A graded linear series \(V_\bullet = \{V_m\}_{m \ge 0}\) on \(X\) associated with a Cartier divisor \(D \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\) (or line bundle \(L = \mathcal{O}_X(D)\)) consists of a collection of finite-dimensional vector subspaces: \[
V_m \subseteq H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)), \quad m \ge 0,
\] such that \(V_0 = \mathbb{C}\) and for all \(k, \ell \ge 0\), the natural multiplication of sections satisfies: \[
V_k \cdot V_\ell := \operatorname{Im}\big(V_k \otimes_{\mathbb{C}} V_\ell \longrightarrow H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X((k+\ell)D))\big) \subseteq V_{k+\ell}.
\]
The direct sum: \[
R(V_\bullet) := \bigoplus_{m=0}^\infty V_m
\] forms a graded \(\mathbb{C}\)-subalgebra of the complete section ring \(R(X, D) = \bigoplus_{m=0}^\infty H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD))\), called the section ring associated with \(V_\bullet\).



Definition 2 (Finite Generation) A graded linear series \(V_\bullet\) on a projective variety \(X\) is said to be finitely generated if its associated section ring \(R(V_\bullet)\) is finitely generated as a \(\mathbb{C}\)-algebra.


Definition 3 (Graded Linear Series Associated with an Ideal Sheaf) Let \(\mathfrak{b} \subseteq \mathcal{O}_X\) be a non-zero ideal sheaf, and let \(c \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\). Setting: \[
V_m := H^0\big(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD) \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathfrak{b}^{\lceil m c \rceil}\big),
\] the collection \(V_\bullet = \{V_m\}_{m \ge 0}\) forms a graded linear series because \(\lceil k c \rceil + \lceil \ell c \rceil \ge \lceil (k+\ell)c \rceil\), which guarantees that \(\mathfrak{b}^{\lceil k c \rceil} \cdot \mathfrak{b}^{\lceil \ell c \rceil} \subseteq \mathfrak{b}^{\lceil (k+\ell)c \rceil}\). This series is denoted by: \[
V_\bullet = \Gamma\big(X, \mathcal{O}_X(D) \otimes \mathfrak{b}^c\big).
\]


Definition 4 (Linear Series Restricted to a Subvariety) Let \(X \subseteq Y\) be an irreducible subvariety and \(D' \in \operatorname{Div}(Y)\) a Cartier divisor on \(Y\) such that \(D = D'|_X\) is well-defined. The trace linear series on \(X\) is defined by: \[
V_m := \operatorname{Im}\big(H^0(Y, \mathcal{O}_Y(mD')) \longrightarrow H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD))\big),
\] and is denoted by \(V_\bullet = \operatorname{Tr}_X(D')\).


Definition 5 (Operations on Graded Linear Series)  

Product: If \(V_\bullet\) and \(W_\bullet\) are graded linear series associated with \(D\) and \(E\) respectively, their product \((V \cdot W)_\bullet\) is defined by: \[
(V \cdot W)_m := \operatorname{Im}\big(V_m \otimes W_m \longrightarrow H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(m(D+E)))\big).
\]
Intersection and Span: If \(V_\bullet, W_\bullet\) are both associated with \(D\), we define: \[
(V \cap W)_m := V_m \cap W_m, \qquad \operatorname{Span}(V_\bullet, W_\bullet)_m := \sum_{k+\ell=m} V_k \cdot W_\ell.
\]
Veronese Subseries: For an integer \(p \ge 1\), the \(p\)-th Veronese subseries is: \[
(V^{(p)})_m := V_{m p},
\] which is associated with \(p D\).



Lemma 1 (Finite Generation of Graded Algebras) Let \(R = \bigoplus_{i=0}^\infty R_i\) be a graded algebra over a Noetherian domain \(R_0\).

\(R\) is a finitely generated \(R_0\)-algebra if and only if the Veronese subring \(R^{(m)} = \bigoplus_{k=0}^\infty R_{k m}\) is a finitely generated \(R_0\)-algebra for any \(m \ge 1\).
If \(R\) is a finitely generated \(R_0\)-algebra, then there exists an integer \(p \ge 1\) such that \(R^{(p)}\) is generated in degree 1 by \(R_p\).



Theorem 1 (Preservation of Finite Generation) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety.

If \(V_\bullet\) and \(W_\bullet\) are finitely generated, then \((V \cdot W)_\bullet\) is finitely generated.
If \(V_\bullet\) and \(W_\bullet\) are finitely generated, then \(\operatorname{Span}(V_\bullet, W_\bullet)\) is finitely generated.
\(V_\bullet\) is finitely generated if and only if \(V^{(p)}\) is finitely generated for any \(p \ge 1\).



Proof. Statements (2) and (3) follow directly from standard commutative algebra and Lemma 1.
For (1), by Lemma 1, it suffices to show that the Veronese subseries \(((V \cdot W)^{(p)})_\bullet\) is finitely generated for some \(p \ge 1\). Choose \(m \gg 0\) such that both \(R(V_\bullet)^{(m)}\) and \(R(W_\bullet)^{(m)}\) are generated in degree 1. Suppose \(V_m\) is spanned by \(f_1, \dots, f_a\) and \(W_m\) is spanned by \(g_1, \dots, g_b\). Then the degree-\(k\) piece \((V \cdot W)_{k m}\) is spanned by elements of the form: \[
\left(\prod_{i=1}^a f_i^{\alpha_i}\right) \cdot \left(\prod_{j=1}^b g_j^{\beta_j}\right), \quad \sum_{i=1}^a \alpha_i = k, \; \sum_{j=1}^b \beta_j = k.
\] Every such monomial can be regrouped into a product of \(k\) terms of the form \(f_i g_j \in V_m \cdot W_m\). Hence \(R((V \cdot W)_\bullet)^{(m)}\) is generated in degree 1 by \(V_m \cdot W_m\). Therefore, \((V \cdot W)_\bullet\) is finitely generated.


Definition 6 (Semigroups, Iitaka Dimension, and Stable Base Locus) Let \(V_\bullet\) be a graded linear series on \(X\).

The semigroup of non-zero multiples is \(N(V_\bullet) := \{ m \ge 0 \mid V_m \neq 0 \}\) with exponent \(e(V_\bullet) = e(N(V_\bullet))\). The semigroup of free multiples is \(M(V_\bullet) := \{ m \ge 0 \mid |V_m| \text{ is base-point-free} \}\) with exponent \(f(V_\bullet) = e(M(V_\bullet))\).
The Iitaka dimension of \(V_\bullet\) is defined by: \[
\kappa(V_\bullet) := \begin{cases} \max_{m \in N(V_\bullet)} \big\{ \dim \overline{\phi_m(X)} \big\}, & N(V_\bullet) \neq \{0\}, \\ -\infty, & V_m = 0 \text{ for all } m > 0, \end{cases}
\] where \(\phi_m: X \dashrightarrow \mathbb{P} V_m\) is the rational map given by \(|V_m|\).
The stable base locus of \(V_\bullet\) is the algebraic subset: \[
\mathbf{B}(V_\bullet) := \bigcap_{m \ge 0} \operatorname{Bs}(|V_m|).
\]
The volume of \(V_\bullet\) is defined by: \[
\operatorname{vol}(V_\bullet) := \limsup_{m \in N(V_\bullet), \, m \to \infty} \frac{\dim_{\mathbb{C}} V_m}{m^n / n!}, \quad \text{where } n = \dim X.
\]



Example 1 (Graded Linear Series with Irrational Volume) Let \(x = [1:0:\dots:0] \in \mathbb{P}^n\), and let \(\mathfrak{m} = \mathcal{I}_{x/\mathbb{P}^n}\) be its maximal ideal sheaf. For a fixed real number \(0 < c < 1\), consider the graded linear series: \[
V_\bullet = \Gamma\big(\mathbb{P}^n, \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^n}(1) \otimes \mathfrak{m}^c\big), \quad V_p = H^0\big(\mathbb{P}^n, \mathcal{O}(p) \otimes \mathfrak{m}^{\lceil p c \rceil}\big).
\] In homogeneous coordinates, \(V_p\) consists of homogeneous polynomials \(\sum a_\alpha x^\alpha\) of degree \(p\) satisfying \(\alpha_1 + \dots + \alpha_n \ge \lceil p c \rceil\), which is equivalent to \(\alpha_0 \le p - \lceil p c \rceil\). Thus: \[
\dim_{\mathbb{C}} V_p = \binom{n+p}{n} - \binom{n + \lceil p c \rceil - 1}{n} = \frac{1}{n!} (p^n - c^n p^n) + O(p^{n-1}).
\] Hence the volume is given by: \[
\operatorname{vol}(V_\bullet) = 1 - c^n.
\] Taking \(n = 3\) and \(c = 1/\sqrt{2}\), we obtain \(\operatorname{vol}(V_\bullet) = 1 - \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \notin \mathbb{Q}\), yielding an irrational volume.



Definition 7 (Graded Families of Ideals)  

A graded family of ideals on an irreducible variety \(X\) is a sequence \(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet = \{\mathfrak{a}_m\}_{m \ge 0}\) of ideal sheaves \(\mathfrak{a}_m \subseteq \mathcal{O}_X\) such that \(\mathfrak{a}_0 = \mathcal{O}_X\) and: \[
\mathfrak{a}_k \cdot \mathfrak{a}_\ell \subseteq \mathfrak{a}_{k+\ell} \quad \text{for all } k, \ell \ge 0.
\]
The Rees algebra of \(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet\) is the graded \(\mathcal{O}_X\)-algebra \(\operatorname{Rees}(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet) := \bigoplus_{m \ge 0} \mathfrak{a}_m\). The family \(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet\) is finitely generated if \(\operatorname{Rees}(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet)\) is a finitely generated \(\mathcal{O}_X\)-algebra.
For an ideal \(\mathfrak{b} \subseteq \mathcal{O}_X\), the trivial family \(\mathfrak{a}_m = \mathfrak{b}^m\) is denoted by \(\operatorname{Pow}_\bullet(\mathfrak{b})\).
For any graded linear series \(V_\bullet\), the base ideals \(\mathfrak{b}_m := \mathfrak{b}(|V_m|)\) form a graded family of ideals, denoted \(\mathfrak{b}(V_\bullet)\).



Definition 8 (Operations and Semigroups for Graded Ideals) For graded families of ideals \(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet\) and \(\mathfrak{b}_\bullet\): \[
(\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b})_m := \mathfrak{a}_m \cap \mathfrak{b}_m, \qquad (\mathfrak{a} \cdot \mathfrak{b})_m := \mathfrak{a}_m \cdot \mathfrak{b}_m, \qquad (\mathfrak{a} + \mathfrak{b})_m := \sum_{k+\ell=m} \mathfrak{a}_k \cdot \mathfrak{b}_\ell, \qquad (\mathfrak{a}^{(p)})_m := \mathfrak{a}_{m p}.
\] The non-zero semigroup is \(N(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet) := \{ m \ge 0 \mid \mathfrak{a}_m \neq (0) \}\) with exponent \(e(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet) = e(N(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet))\).


Proposition 1 (Powers of Finitely Generated Graded Ideals) If \(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet = \{\mathfrak{a}_m\}_{m \ge 0}\) is a finitely generated graded family of ideals, then there exists an integer \(p \ge 1\) such that: \[
\mathfrak{a}_\bullet^{(p)} = \operatorname{Pow}_\bullet(\mathfrak{a}_p), \quad \text{that is}, \quad \mathfrak{a}_{m p} = (\mathfrak{a}_p)^m \quad \text{for all } m \ge 1.
\]


Proof. By Lemma 1, the Rees algebra \(\operatorname{Rees}(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet)^{(p)}\) is generated in degree 1 for some \(p \ge 1\). Hence its degree-\(m\) piece is given by the \(m\)-th power of its degree-1 piece: \(\mathfrak{a}_{m p} = (\mathfrak{a}_p)^m\).


Lemma 2 (Castelnuovo-Mumford Regularity) Let \(X\) be a projective scheme and \(B\) an ample line bundle on \(X\). A coherent sheaf \(\mathcal{F}\) is said to be \(m\)-regular with respect to \(B\) if \(H^i(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes B^{\otimes(m-i)}) = 0\) for all \(i \ge 1\). If \(\mathcal{F}\) is \(m\)-regular, then for every \(k \ge 0\):

\(\mathcal{F} \otimes B^{\otimes(m+k)}\) is generated by its global sections;
The multiplication map on global sections is surjective: \[
H^0(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes B^{\otimes m}) \otimes H^0(X, B^{\otimes k}) \twoheadrightarrow H^0(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes B^{\otimes(m+k)});
\]
\(\mathcal{F}\) is \((m+k)\)-regular with respect to \(B\).



Proposition 2 (Finite Generation for Semiample Bundles and Base Ideals) Let \(X\) be a normal projective variety.

If \(L\) is a base-point-free line bundle on \(X\), then there exists an integer \(m_0 \ge 1\) such that for all \(a, b \ge m_0\), the multiplication map: \[
H^0(X, L^{\otimes a}) \otimes H^0(X, L^{\otimes b}) \longrightarrow H^0(X, L^{\otimes(a+b)})
\] is surjective.
If \(L\) is semiample, then \(R(X, L)\) is a finitely generated \(\mathbb{C}\)-algebra.
Let \(D \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\). If the graded family of base ideals \(\mathfrak{b}_\bullet = \{\mathfrak{b}(|mD|)\}_{m \ge 0}\) is finitely generated, then the section ring \(R(X, D)\) is finitely generated.



Proof. Proof of (1): Let \(\phi: X \to Y\) be the semiample fibration associated with \(L\) (?@thm-semiample-fibration), so that \(\phi_* \mathcal{O}_X = \mathcal{O}_Y\) and \(L \cong \phi^* A\) for an ample line bundle \(A\) on \(Y\) (assuming \(f(L) = 1\)). By the projection formula, \(H^0(X, L^{\otimes m}) \cong H^0(Y, A^{\otimes m})\). Since \(A\) is ample, it is \(m_0\)-regular for some \(m_0 \gg 0\). By Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity (Lemma 2), multiplication of sections is surjective on \(Y\), hence on \(X\).
Proof of (2): Choose \(n \ge 1\) such that \(L^{\otimes n}\) is base-point-free. By (1), the Veronese subring \(R(X, L^{\otimes n})^{(m_0)} = R(X, L^{\otimes n m_0})\) is generated in degree 1. Hence \(R(X, L^{\otimes n m_0})\) is finitely generated, and by Lemma 1, \(R(X, L)\) is finitely generated.
Proof of (3): By Proposition 1, replacing \(D\) by a multiple \(p D\), we may assume \(\mathfrak{b}(|mD|) = \mathfrak{b}_1^m\) for all \(m \ge 1\). Let \(\nu: X^+ \to X\) be the normalization of the blow-up \(\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathfrak{b}_1}(X)\), let \(N^+\) be the exceptional divisor on \(X^+\), and set \(D^+ := \nu^* D - N^+\). As in the proof of ?@thm-iitaka-fibration, \(D^+\) is base-point-free, so \(R(X^+, D^+)\) is finitely generated by (2). Furthermore, because \(\mathfrak{b}(|mD|) = \mathfrak{b}_1^m\), the pullback of the base locus is precisely \(m N^+\), which implies that all global sections of \(\nu^* (mD)\) vanish along \(m N^+\). Thus: \[
H^0(X^+, \mathcal{O}_{X^+}(m D^+)) \cong H^0(X^+, \mathcal{O}_{X^+}(m \nu^* D)) \cong H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)).
\] Consequently, \(R(X^+, D^+) \cong R(X, D)\), proving that \(R(X, D)\) is finitely generated.


Definition 9 (Multiplicity of a Graded System of Ideals) Let \(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet = \{\mathfrak{a}_m\}_{m \ge 0}\) be a graded system of \(\mathfrak{m}_x\)-primary ideals at a closed point \(x \in X\). The multiplicity of \(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet\) is defined by: \[
\operatorname{mult}(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet) := \lim_{m \to \infty} \frac{\operatorname{length}_{\mathcal{O}_{X, x}}(\mathcal{O}_{X, x} / \mathfrak{a}_m)}{m^n / n!}.
\]


Theorem 2 (Wilson’s Theorem) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety of dimension \(n\), and let \(D\) be a nef and big Cartier divisor on \(X\). Then there exists an integer \(m_0 \ge 1\) and an effective Cartier divisor \(N\) such that the linear system: \[
|m D - N|
\] is base-point-free for all \(m \ge m_0\).


Proof. By Fujita’s Vanishing Theorem (?@thm-fujita-vanishing), there exists a very ample divisor \(B\) such that for all \(i > 0\) and any nef divisor \(P\), \(H^i(X, \mathcal{O}_X(B + P)) = 0\). Since \(D\) is big, ?@cor-characterization-bigness implies that there exists an integer \(m_0 > 0\) and an effective divisor \(N\) such that: \[
N \sim m_0 D - (n+1)B.
\] For any \(m \ge m_0\), we rewrite: \[
m D - N \sim (m - m_0)D + (n+1)B = B + n B + (m - m_0)D.
\] For each \(1 \le i \le n\), the divisor \((m D - N) - i B \sim B + (n-i)B + (m-m_0)D\) has the form \(B + P\) with \(P = (n-i)B + (m-m_0)D\) nef. Thus: \[
H^i\big(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD - N - i B)\big) = 0 \quad \text{for all } 1 \le i \le n.
\] Therefore, \(\mathcal{O}_X(m D - N)\) is 0-regular with respect to \(B\). By Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity (Lemma 2), \(|m D - N|\) is base-point-free.


Definition 10 (Multiplicity of a Linear System at a Point) Let \(X\) be a projective variety and \(x \in X\) a fixed point. For any linear system \(|V| \subseteq |D|\), the multiplicity of \(|V|\) at \(x\) is: \[
\operatorname{mult}_x |V| := \min_{D' \in |V|} \big\{ \operatorname{mult}_x(D') \big\}.
\]


Proposition 3 (Uniform Boundedness of Multiplicities) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety of dimension \(n\), and let \(D\) be a nef and big Cartier divisor. Then for any point \(x \in X\), there exists a constant \(C > 0\) and an integer \(m_0\) such that: \[
\operatorname{mult}_x |m D| \le C \quad \text{for all } m \ge m_0.
\]


Proof. By Wilson’s Theorem (Theorem 2), there exist \(m_0\) and an effective divisor \(N\) such that \(|m D - N|\) is free for all \(m \ge m_0\). Choose an element \(E \in |m D - N|\) not passing through \(x\), so that \(\operatorname{mult}_x(E) = 0\). Then \(E + N \in |m D|\), which yields: \[
\operatorname{mult}_x |m D| \le \operatorname{mult}_x(E + N) = \operatorname{mult}_x(N) =: C.
\]


Theorem 3 (Criterion for Finite Generation of Section Rings) Let \(X\) be a normal projective variety, and let \(D\) be a nef and big Cartier divisor on \(X\). Then: \[
R(X, D) \text{ is finitely generated} \iff D \text{ is semiample}.
\]


Proof. \((\impliedby)\): This is Proposition 2(2).
\((\implies)\): Assume \(R(X, D)\) is finitely generated. By Lemma 1, there exists an integer \(\ell \ge 1\) such that \(R(X, D)^{(\ell)}\) is generated in degree 1 by \(H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(\ell D))\). Consequently, the natural symmetric algebra evaluation: \[
\operatorname{Sym}^k H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(\ell D)) \twoheadrightarrow H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(k \ell D))
\] is surjective for all \(k \ge 1\). This implies that every element in \(|k \ell D|\) is a sum of \(k\) elements from \(|\ell D|\), whence: \[
\operatorname{mult}_x |k \ell D| \ge k \cdot \operatorname{mult}_x |\ell D|.
\] However, by Proposition 3, the left-hand side is bounded by a constant \(C\) independent of \(k\). Letting \(k \to \infty\) forces: \[
\operatorname{mult}_x |\ell D| = 0.
\] Since this holds for every closed point \(x \in X\), the linear system \(|\ell D|\) has no base points. Hence \(D\) is semiample.

title: 22.1 Nef-Divisors
text:
Theorem 1 (Nakai-Moishezon Criterion) Let \(X\) be a projective scheme and \(L\) a line bundle on \(X\). Then \(L\) is ample if and only if for every irreducible subvariety \(V \subseteq X\) with \(\dim V \ge 1\), \[
(L^{\dim V} \cdot V) > 0.
\]


Proof. \((\implies)\): Suppose \(L\) is ample. Then \(L^{\otimes m}\) is very ample for some \(m \ge 1\). For any irreducible subvariety \(V \subseteq X\) of dimension \(k = \dim V \ge 1\), \[
((L^{\otimes m})^k \cdot V) = m^k (L^k \cdot V).
\] The very ample line bundle \(L^{\otimes m}\) defines an embedding \(X \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^N\) such that \(L^{\otimes m} \cong \mathcal{O}_X(1)\). Then: \[
((L^{\otimes m})^k \cdot V) = (\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^N}(1)^k \cdot V) = \deg(V) > 0.
\] Since \(m^k > 0\), we conclude that \((L^k \cdot V) > 0\).
\((\impliedby)\): By ?@prp-amplitude-checked-curves(2), we may assume without loss of generality that \(X\) is integral. We proceed by induction on \(n = \dim X\):

If \(\dim X = 1\), \(L\) is ample if and only if \(\deg L = (L \cdot X) > 0\), which holds by hypothesis.
Assume the criterion holds for all schemes of dimension \(\le n - 1\).
Let \(L = \mathcal{O}_X(D)\) for some Cartier divisor \(D \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\).

Step 1: \(H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) \neq 0\) for \(m \gg 0\). By Asymptotic Riemann-Roch (?@thm-asymptotic-rr-1), \[
\chi(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}).
\] Since \((D^n) = (D^n \cdot X) > 0\), the leading coefficient is strictly positive.
Write \(L = M \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} N^\vee\) with \(M, N\) very ample line bundles on \(X\). Choosing effective divisors \(A, B\) such that \(M \cong \mathcal{O}_X(A)\) and \(N \cong \mathcal{O}_X(B)\), we have \(D \sim A - B\).
Tensoring the short exact sequence \(0 \to \mathcal{O}_X(-A) \to \mathcal{O}_X \to \mathcal{O}_A \to 0\) with \(\mathcal{O}_X((m+1)D)\) yields: \[
0 \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X(mD - B) \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X((m+1)D) \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_A((m+1)D) \longrightarrow 0,
\] since \((m+1)D - A = mD + (D - A) \sim mD - B\). Similarly, tensoring \(0 \to \mathcal{O}_X(-B) \to \mathcal{O}_X \to \mathcal{O}_B \to 0\) with \(\mathcal{O}_X(mD)\) yields: \[
0 \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X(mD - B) \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X(mD) \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_B(mD) \longrightarrow 0.
\] Because \(\dim A, \dim B \le n-1\), the induction hypothesis applies to the restricted bundles on \(A\) and \(B\), implying that for \(m \gg 0\), their higher cohomology stabilizes. Consequently: \[
H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) \cong H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD - B)) \cong H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X((m+1)D))
\] for \(m \gg 0\), meaning \(\dim H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD))\) is bounded. Therefore: \[
\chi(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) - h^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) + O(1) \longrightarrow +\infty \quad \text{as } m \to \infty,
\] which forces \(h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) > 0\) for all \(m \gg 0\).
Step 2: \(\mathcal{O}_X(mD)\) is globally generated for \(m \gg 0\). Replacing \(D\) by a linearly equivalent effective divisor \(D' \sim mD\) (noting that \(D\) is ample if and only if \(mD\) is ample), we may assume \(D \ge 0\).
To show \(\mathcal{O}_X(mD)\) is globally generated, it suffices to show that the evaluation map: \[
H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) \otimes_k \mathcal{O}_{X, P} \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X(mD)_P
\] is surjective for every point \(P \in X\). - If \(P \notin \operatorname{Supp}(D)\), the canonical section \(s_D^{\otimes m}\) does not vanish at \(P\), so surjectivity holds trivially. - For \(P \in \operatorname{Supp}(D)\), consider the exact sequence: \[
  0 \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X((m-1)D) \xrightarrow{\;\times D\;} \mathcal{O}_X(mD) \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_D(mD) \longrightarrow 0.
  \] Since \(\dim D = n - 1\), the induction hypothesis implies \(\mathcal{O}_D(D)\) is ample on \(D\). Hence \(\mathcal{O}_D(mD)\) is globally generated and \(H^1(D, \mathcal{O}_D(mD)) = 0\) for \(m \gg 0\). The long exact sequence shows: \[
  H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X((m-1)D)) \longrightarrow H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD))
  \] is surjective for all large \(m\). Thus the dimension sequence \(\dim_k H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD))\) is non-increasing, hence constant for \(m \ge m_0\): \[
  H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X((m-1)D)) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)).
  \] This yields a surjection on global sections: \[
  H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) \twoheadrightarrow H^0(D, \mathcal{O}_D(mD)).
  \] Considering the commutative diagram: \[
  \begin{CD}
  H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) @>>> H^0(D, \mathcal{O}_D(mD)) \\
  @VVV @VVV \\
  \mathcal{O}_X(mD)_P @>>> \mathcal{O}_D(mD) \otimes k(P) \cong \mathcal{O}_X(mD) \otimes k(P)
  \end{CD}
  \] Since \(\mathcal{O}_D(mD)\) is globally generated, the right vertical arrow is surjective, which implies that \(\mathcal{O}_X(mD)\) is generated by global sections at every \(P \in \operatorname{Supp}(D)\).
Finally, because \(\mathcal{O}_X(mD)\) is globally generated and satisfies \((mD \cdot C) > 0\) for all irreducible curves \(C \subseteq X\), ?@prp-amplitude-checked-curves(3) implies that \(\mathcal{O}_X(mD)\) is ample. Hence \(L\) is ample.



Definition 1 (\(\mathbb{Q}\)-Divisors)  

Let \(X\) be a scheme over \(k\). The group of \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Cartier divisors is: \[
\operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X) := \operatorname{Div}(X) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q}.
\] Every \(D \in \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X)\) can be written as \(D = \frac{1}{n} A\) for some \(n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) and \(A \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\).
A \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisor \(D\) is integral if it lies in the image of the natural map \(\operatorname{Div}(X) \to \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X)\).
A \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisor \(D\) is effective (\(D \ge 0\)) if it can be written as \(D = \sum c_i A_i\) with rational coefficients \(c_i > 0\) and effective Cartier divisors \(A_i\) (equivalently, \(D = c A\) for some \(c \in \mathbb{Q}_{>0}\) and effective \(A \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\)).



Definition 2 (Support of \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Divisors) Let \(D \in \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X)\). A codimension 1 closed subscheme \(E \subseteq X\) is said to support \(D\) if there exists a representation \(D = \sum c_i A_i\) such that \(\bigcup_i \operatorname{Supp}(A_i) \subseteq E\).


Definition 3 (Intersection and Equivalence of \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Divisors) Let \(X\) be a proper scheme.

Let \(V \subseteq X\) be a subscheme of pure dimension \(k\). The \(\mathbb{Q}\)-valued intersection product is defined by multi-linear extension: \[
\operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X)^k \longrightarrow \mathbb{Q}, \quad (D_1, \dots, D_k) \longmapsto \prod_{i=1}^k c_i \cdot (A_1 \cdots A_k \cdot [V]),
\] where \(D_i = c_i A_i\) with \(c_i \in \mathbb{Q}\) and \(A_i \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\).
Two \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisors \(D_1, D_2\) are numerically equivalent (denoted \(D_1 \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} D_2\)) if \((D_1 \cdot C) = (D_2 \cdot C)\) for every irreducible curve \(C \subseteq X\). We set: \[
N^1(X)_{\mathbb{Q}} := N^1(X) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q}.
\]
Two \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisors \(D_1, D_2\) are \(\mathbb{Q}\)-linearly equivalent (denoted \(D_1 \sim_{\mathbb{Q}} D_2\) or \(D_1 \equiv_{\mathrm{lin}} D_2\)) if there exists an integer \(r > 0\) such that \(r D_1, r D_2\) are integral and \(r D_1 \sim r D_2\). We set: \[
\operatorname{CaCl}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X) := \operatorname{CaCl}(X) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q}.
\]



Definition 4 (Ample \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Divisors) A \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisor \(D \in \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X)\) is ample if it satisfies any of the following three equivalent conditions:

\(D = \sum c_i A_i\) with \(c_i \in \mathbb{Q}_{>0}\) and each \(A_i \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\) ample;
There exists an integer \(r > 0\) such that \(r D\) is an integral ample Cartier divisor;
\((D^{\dim V} \cdot V) > 0\) for all irreducible subvarieties \(V \subseteq X\) with \(\dim V \ge 1\).



Proposition 1 (Openness of Amplitude for \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Divisors) Let \(X\) be a projective variety, and let \(H\) be an ample \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisor on \(X\). For any \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisors \(E_1, \dots, E_r\), the perturbed divisor: \[
H + \varepsilon_1 E_1 + \dots + \varepsilon_r E_r
\] is ample for all rational numbers \(\varepsilon_i\) satisfying \(0 \le |\varepsilon_i| \ll 1\).


Proof. Clearing denominators, we may assume without loss of generality that \(H\) and each \(E_i\) are integral Cartier divisors. Because \(H\) is ample, there exists an integer \(m \gg 0\) such that \(m H \pm E_i\) is ample for each \(i = 1, \dots, r\). Rewriting the perturbation as a convex linear combination: \[
H + \sum_{i=1}^r \varepsilon_i E_i = \sum_{i=1}^r |\varepsilon_i| \cdot \frac{1}{m}\big(m H + \operatorname{sgn}(\varepsilon_i) E_i\big) + \left(1 - \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^r |\varepsilon_i|\right) H.
\] For \(\sum_{i=1}^r |\varepsilon_i| < m\), this is a positive rational linear combination of ample divisors, hence ample.



Definition 5 (\(\mathbb{R}\)-Divisors)  

The real vector space of \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisors is: \[
\operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{R}}(X) := \operatorname{Div}(X) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{R}.
\] The intersection product extends multi-linearly to \((D_1 \cdots D_k \cdot V) \in \mathbb{R}\). Two \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisors \(D_1, D_2\) are numerically equivalent (\(D_1 \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} D_2\)) if \((D_1 \cdot C) = (D_2 \cdot C)\) for every curve \(C\).
The real Néron-Severi space is defined by: \[
N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} := \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{R}}(X) / \equiv_{\mathrm{num}}.
\]
An \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor \(D\) is effective if \(D = \sum c_i A_i\) with \(c_i \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) and \(A_i\) effective Cartier divisors.
An \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor \(D\) is ample if \(D = \sum c_i A_i\) with \(c_i \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}\) and \(A_i\) ample integral Cartier divisors.



Proposition 2 (Flat Base Change for \(N^1(X)\)) There is a canonical identification: \[
N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} = N^1(X) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{R} = N^1(X)_{\mathbb{Q}} \otimes_{\mathbb{Q}} \mathbb{R}.
\]


Proof. Since \(\mathbb{R}\) is a flat \(\mathbb{Z}\)-module, it suffices to show that: \[
\big\{ D \in \operatorname{Div}(X) \mid D \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} 0 \big\} \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{R} = \big\{ D \in \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{R}}(X) \mid D \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} 0 \big\}.
\] The inclusion \(\subseteq\) is evident. Conversely, let \(D = \sum_{i=1}^k c_i A_i\) with \(c_i \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(A_i \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\) satisfy \((D \cdot C) = 0\) for all curves \(C \subseteq X\). The intersection pairing defines a linear map: \[
\phi: \mathbb{Z}^k \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}^{A_1(X)}, \quad (a_1, \dots, a_k) \longmapsto \left( C \mapsto \sum_{i=1}^k a_i (A_i \cdot C) \right).
\] Since \((c_1, \dots, c_k) \in \ker(\phi \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{R})\), we have \(\ker(\phi \otimes \mathbb{Q}) \neq 0\), so \(\ker(\phi) \neq 0\). Choose a non-zero vector \((a_1, \dots, a_k) \in \mathbb{Z}^k \cap \ker(\phi)\) with \(a_1 \neq 0\). The divisor \(A_1' := \sum a_i A_i\) satisfies \(A_1' \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} 0\). We then decompose: \[
D = \frac{c_1}{a_1} A_1' + \sum_{i=2}^k \left(c_i - \frac{c_1 a_i}{a_1}\right) A_i.
\] The second term involves only \(k - 1\) divisors and is numerically trivial. Induction on \(k\) proves \(D \in \{ D \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} 0 \} \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{R}\).


Definition 6 (1-Cycles Modulo Numerical Equivalence)  

Let \(X\) be a proper scheme. Define the real vector space of 1-cycles by: \[
Z_1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} := \bigoplus_{C \subseteq X \text{ curve}} \mathbb{R} \cdot C.
\] Two 1-cycles \(\gamma_1, \gamma_2\) are numerically equivalent (\(\gamma_1 \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} \gamma_2\)) if \((D \cdot \gamma_1) = (D \cdot \gamma_2)\) for all \(D \in \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{R}}(X)\). We define: \[
N_1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} := Z_1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} / \equiv_{\mathrm{num}}.
\] Then the intersection pairing induces a perfect pairing of finite-dimensional real vector spaces: \[
N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} \times N_1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}, \quad (\delta, \gamma) \longmapsto (\delta \cdot \gamma).
\]
Both \(N_1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\) and \(N_1(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}\) are finite-dimensional, and \(N_1(X)\) is a finitely generated free abelian group.



Proposition 3 (Openness of Amplitude for \(\mathbb{R}\)-Divisors)  

If \(D_1 \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} D_2\), then \(D_1\) is ample if and only if \(D_2\) is ample.
If \(H \in \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{R}}(X)\) is ample, then \(H + \varepsilon_1 E_1 + \dots + \varepsilon_r E_r\) is ample for all \(0 \le |\varepsilon_i| \ll 1\). In particular, the ample cone \(\operatorname{Amp}(X) \subseteq N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\) is open.




Definition 7 (Nef Divisors)  

Let \(X\) be a proper scheme. A line bundle \(L \in \operatorname{Pic}(X)\) is numerically effective (nef) if for every irreducible curve \(C \subseteq X\), \[
(L \cdot C) \ge 0.
\] An \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor \(D \in \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{R}}(X)\) is nef if \((D \cdot C) \ge 0\) for all irreducible curves \(C \subseteq X\).
Nefness depends only on the numerical class: if \(D_1 \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} D_2\), then \(D_1\) is nef if and only if \(D_2\) is nef.



Proposition 4 (Functorial Properties of Nef Bundles)  

Let \(f: X \to Y\) be a proper morphism. If \(L \in \operatorname{Pic}(Y)\) is nef, then \(f^* L\) is nef on \(X\). If \(f\) is additionally surjective, then \(L\) is nef if and only if \(f^* L\) is nef.
If \(L\) is globally generated, then \(L\) is nef. In particular, the pullback of \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(1)\) under any morphism \(\phi_{|L|}: X \to \mathbb{P}^N\) is nef.
\(L\) is nef if and only if \(L|_{X_{\mathrm{red}}}\) is nef, if and only if \(L|_{X_i}\) is nef for every irreducible component \(X_i \subseteq X\).



Theorem 2 (Kleiman’s Theorem) Let \(X\) be a proper scheme and \(D \in \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{R}}(X)\) a nef \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor. Then for every irreducible subvariety \(V \subseteq X\) of dimension \(k = \dim V\), \[
(D^k \cdot V) \ge 0.
\]


Proof. By Proposition 4(3), we may assume \(X\) is irreducible and reduced.
Reduction to the projective case: By Chow’s Lemma, there exists a projective variety \(\widetilde{X}\) and a birational surjective morphism \(f: \widetilde{X} \to X\). For any curve \(C \subseteq \widetilde{X}\), by the projection formula: \[
(f^* D \cdot C) = (D \cdot f_* C) \ge 0,
\] so \(f^* D\) is nef on \(\widetilde{X}\). If the theorem holds for projective varieties, then for any \(V \subseteq X\) of dimension \(k\), choosing \(V' \subseteq \widetilde{X}\) such that \(f_* V' = \deg(V'/V) V\), we have: \[
(D^k \cdot V) = \frac{1}{\deg(V'/V)} ((f^* D)^k \cdot V') \ge 0.
\] Thus we may assume \(X\) is projective.
We induct on \(n = \dim X\): - If \(n = 1\), \((D \cdot X) \ge 0\) by the definition of nefness. - Assume the result holds in dimensions \(\le n - 1\). For any proper subvariety \(V \subsetneq X\) of dimension \(k \le n - 1\), \(D|_V\) is nef, so \((D^k \cdot V) \ge 0\) by induction. It remains to show that \((D^n) = (D^n \cdot X) \ge 0\).
Case 1: \(D\) is a \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisor. Fix an ample divisor \(H\) on \(X\), and consider the polynomial: \[
P(t) := ((D + t H)^n) = \sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i} (D^{n-i} \cdot H^i) t^i = a_n t^n + a_{n-1} t^{n-1} + \dots + a_0.
\] By induction, for \(1 \le i \le n\), the cycle \(H^i\) is represented by a positive combination of \((n-i)\)-dimensional subvarieties, so \(a_i = \binom{n}{i} (D^{n-i} \cdot H^i) \ge 0\), and \(a_n = (H^n) > 0\).
Suppose toward a contradiction that \(a_0 = (D^n) < 0\). By Descartes’ rule of signs, \(P(t)\) has a unique positive root \(t_0 > 0\).
Claim: For any rational \(t > t_0\), the divisor \(D + t H\) is ample. We verify the Nakai-Moishezon criterion (Theorem 1): - For \(V = X\), \(((D + t H)^n \cdot X) = P(t) > 0\) because \(t > t_0\) and \(a_n > 0\). - For any subvariety \(V \subsetneq X\) of dimension \(k < n\), the expansion: \[
  ((D + t H)^k \cdot V) = (D^k \cdot V) + \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} \binom{k}{i} (D^{k-i} \cdot H^i \cdot V) t^i + (H^k \cdot V) t^k
  \] has non-negative coefficients for \(i < k\) by the induction hypothesis, and the leading coefficient satisfies \((H^k \cdot V) > 0\). Thus \(((D + t H)^k \cdot V) > 0\) for all \(t > 0\).
This proves \(D + t H\) is ample for all rational \(t > t_0\). Now decompose \(P(t)\) as: \[
P(t) = Q(t) + R(t), \quad \text{where } Q(t) = (D \cdot (D + t H)^{n-1}), \quad R(t) = t(H \cdot (D + t H)^{n-1}).
\] For \(t > t_0\), \(D + t H\) is ample, so \((D + t H)^{n-1}\) is represented by an effective 1-cycle. Since \(D\) is nef, \(Q(t) \ge 0\) for all \(t > t_0\), and by continuity \(Q(t_0) \ge 0\). Furthermore, every coefficient of \(R(t)\) is non-negative and its leading term \((H^n) t^n\) is strictly positive, so \(R(t_0) > 0\). Hence: \[
P(t_0) = Q(t_0) + R(t_0) > 0,
\] contradicting \(P(t_0) = 0\). Thus \((D^n) \ge 0\).
Case 2: \(D\) is an \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor. Choose ample divisors \(H_1, \dots, H_r\) whose classes span \(N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\). For \(\varepsilon = (\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r)\) with \(\varepsilon_i > 0\), the perturbation: \[
D(\varepsilon) := D + \sum_{i=1}^r \varepsilon_i H_i
\] is nef, and the cone of such perturbations forms an open neighborhood. For any \(\delta > 0\), we may choose \(0 < \varepsilon_i < \delta\) such that \(D(\varepsilon) \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} E\) for some \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisor \(E\). By Case 1, \((D(\varepsilon)^k \cdot V) = (E^k \cdot V) \ge 0\). Taking the limit as \(\varepsilon_i \to 0\) yields: \[
(D^k \cdot V) \ge 0.
\] This completes the proof.


Corollary 1 (Kleiman’s Perturbation and Nefness Criterion) Let \(X\) be a projective scheme.

If \(D\) is a nef \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor and \(H\) is an ample \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor, then \(D + \varepsilon H\) is ample for every \(\varepsilon > 0\).
Conversely, if \(D, H\) are \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisors such that \(D + \varepsilon H\) is ample for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon > 0\), then \(D\) is nef.



Proof. Proof of (2): If \(D + \varepsilon H\) is ample for all \(0 < \varepsilon \ll 1\), then for every irreducible curve \(C \subseteq X\), \[
((D + \varepsilon H) \cdot C) = (D \cdot C) + \varepsilon (H \cdot C) > 0.
\] Taking the limit as \(\varepsilon \to 0^+\) gives \((D \cdot C) \ge 0\), so \(D\) is nef.
Proof of (1): Replacing \(\varepsilon H\) by \(H\), it suffices to prove that \(D + H\) is ample. Let \(V \subseteq X\) be an irreducible subvariety of dimension \(k \ge 1\). Expanding the intersection: \[
((D + H)^k \cdot V) = \sum_{s=0}^k \binom{k}{s} (H^s \cdot D^{k-s} \cdot V).
\] Because \(H\) is ample, \(H^s\) is represented by an effective cycle of dimension \(k - s\). By Kleiman’s Theorem (Theorem 2), \((H^s \cdot D^{k-s} \cdot V) \ge 0\) for all \(s < k\). For \(s = k\), \((H^k \cdot V) > 0\). Hence: \[
((D + H)^k \cdot V) \ge (H^k \cdot V) > 0.
\] If \(D + H\) is a \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisor, Nakai-Moishezon (Theorem 1) implies directly that \(D + H\) is ample.
If \(D + H\) is not rational, choose ample divisors \(H_1, \dots, H_r\) spanning \(N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\). By openness of the ample cone, there exist small \(\varepsilon_i > 0\) such that \(H - \sum \varepsilon_i H_i\) remains ample, and: \[
E := D + H - \sum_{i=1}^r \varepsilon_i H_i \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} E_{\mathbb{Q}}
\] is a rational class. Then \(E\) is ample by the rational case, and: \[
D + H = E + \sum_{i=1}^r \varepsilon_i H_i
\] is a sum of ample \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisors, hence ample.
